Date: Mon, 17 May 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Reserved capacity pricing & contingency question

Hi Vanessa,

Thanks again for the walkthrough last week — Peregrine is excited about using Redwood for our inference layer. Before we lock term and SKU counts for the Reserved capacity, procurement has a couple of open items we need to resolve on the pricing side:

- If Nvidia spot/wholesale GPU costs increase materially over the contract period, what protections or triggers does Redwood offer to avoid the vendor bearing all the cost delta?
- Can we structure a SKU rebalance mid-term if our usage shifts between large and medium models?
- We also need an initial sizing model (SKU counts by family + expected token throughput) so we can map to our internal budget.

Would you be able to share a proposal that outlines a pass-through trigger, a short-term SKU rebalancing process, and a preliminary sizing workbook?

Ashley Park
CTO, Peregrine Analytics
ashley@peregrine-analytics.com

Attachments: none
From: Vanessa Ortiz <vanessa@redwood.com>

Date: Tue, 18 May 2027 10:47:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Reserved capacity pricing & contingency question

Hi Ashley — great questions. I pulled together a short proposal and the sizing workbook for you to review (attached). High level:

1) Price-signal mechanism: we can offer a two-tier protection structure — a fixed discount off list for the committed SKUs with a quarterly true-up tied to an industry GPU index. If the index moves >10% in a quarter, we can either (a) apply a one-time surcharge (capped at 5% of committed spend that quarter) or (b) trigger a credit back if our procurement cost drops. For Peregrine I recommend option (b) + a floor to avoid double-sided volatility.

2) SKU rebalance: allowed once per 12-month period without penalty (subject to capacity availability). For mid-term material shifts (>25% of committed vCPUs or tokens), we can run a rebalance exercise: you submit the new workload mix, Redwood ops runs a capacity-impact analysis and we agree on delta credits or prorated adjustments.

3) Sizing: see fleet_sizing_model.xlsx (tab: Peregrine_Base) — I populated conservative throughput and an initial SKU mix (6x L-large, 12x M-mid, 20x S-small) based on your traffic profile. This maps to an estimated 1.8B tokens/month steady-state.

Next steps I propose: Marcus and Karthik join a short call with Peregrine procurement to table the pricing term-sheet and the pass-through trigger language. I'm also attaching a draft term sheet for finance review.

Thanks,
Vanessa Ortiz
Head of Sales, Redwood Inference
vanessa@redwood.com | +1 415-555-0147

Subject: FW: Reserved capacity pricing & contingency question (pricing term sheet)

Vanessa / Karthik —

I reviewed Vanessa's draft and made finance comments in the attached pricing_term_sheet.pdf. Key points from finance:

- We can accept a quarterly index-based true-up but need a cap both ways: +/- 7.5% per quarter and an annual cap of +/- 12% on list pricing exposure.
- Require a minimum committed spend floor to avoid administrative churn if they downscale (recommend $80k/mo).
- For SKU rebalance, we can allow one free rebalance in 12 months; subsequent rebalances incur a reconfiguration fee (tiers in the PDF).
- Contingency clause: finance wants a mechanism to pass through material supply-driven GPU cost increases. Proposed language: if Redwood's underlying procurement cost (verified via invoice or market feed) increases >15% YoY, parties will engage in negotiated relief (rebate/term extension/price adjustment).

I flagged the sections that need executive signoff in the PDF. Vanessa — if Peregrine pushes for a shorter commitment term (<=6 months) we should run the numbers: likely need either higher unit price or reduced discount.

Marcus Lin
Head of Finance, Redwood Inference
marcus.lin@redwood.com

Thanks Vanessa & Marcus — this is helpful. A couple of clarifications from procurement (copied):

- Peregrine's legal team is only comfortable with 9–12 month commitments for this pilot; full 24-months will require board sign-off. Can Redwood provide a 9-month pilot pricing option with a predefined rollover mechanic?
- For the pass-through trigger, procurement wants a transparent public index (not invoice-only) and a predictable cap schedule so our CFO can model cash-flow. Can Redwood tie the trigger to an agreed public GPU index (we suggest "GPUPulse" or similar) and commit to the +/- cap language from finance?
- Regarding SKU rebalance: we'd like the option to shift up to 30% of SKU units between families mid-term with a single reconciliation run (no reconfiguration fee) provided we give 30 days notice.

On the sizing workbook: procurement raised a question on peak concurrency assumptions on the L-large SKUs (sheet: concurrency). Is that headroom flexible for burst windows?

Ashley / procurement — thanks for the clear asks. Quick answers and next steps: 

- 9-month pilot: we can model a 9-month pilot with a predefined rollover: at month 9, you can either convert to a 24-month standard reserved contract at the agreed unit price or roll month-to-month at a 10% premium to protected pricing for up to 6 months. I will include both options in an updated term sheet.
- Public index: Redwood is open to referencing a public index for the quarterly true-up. We'll propose GPUPulse as the primary feed with an agreed methodology in the appendix. We'll also mirror the +/- 7.5% quarterly and +/-12% annual caps Marcus suggested; those go into finance redlines.
- SKU rebalance: we can allow a single mid-term rebalance up to 30% of SKU units with 30 days notice and no fee; any further rebalances will follow the fee schedule in pricing_term_sheet.pdf.
- Concurrency/burst: L-large SKUs include a 20% burst headroom by default; we can configure an additional burst pool (metered) for scheduled peak windows. I'll have Karthik include burst pool costs in the workbook.

Would Peregrine be available for a 30-minute call on Monday 24 May at 10:00am PT to finalize the rollback/rollover language and index methodology? If that works, I'll send a calendar invite and we will bring final redlines for finance execs.

Thanks — looking forward to closing this out.
